(Monocot) Flower bases of 6, very typical parallel leaf veins, suggesting a monocotyledon. The synephridium suggests that it may be a plant of the order Liliaceae. However, after repeated and careful screening with plant identification software and against images of confirmed observations available on plant net and iNat, we believe that this may in fact be Dianella caerulea, commonly known as Blue flax-lily, in the family Asphodelaceae. very characteristic reflexed petals, very characteristic buds with yellow structures on the margins, racemes, purple oval berries, and overall a very recognisable flower. It is worth noting that this family does not appear to be recorded in the Robinson Book under "Monocots", so I think this family, and this species, may be of very good and unique identification value, and I hope you will draw attention to it. Our Alfalfa plants are herbaceous, with berries, anthers that do not curl after dehiscence, and stamens whose filaments are inflated and papillate at the tips. The flowers are strongly tubular and of mixed reddish-brown-orange colour. Anthers dehiscent through apical pores, filaments attached at or near the base of the anthers, anthers inactive. Leaf blades spreading, flowers borne in axils or not alone at apices; plants non-alpine types. Leaves mostly basal or reduced and bracteate along above-ground stems, flowers often borne on nearly leafless scapes or apical inflorescences. Underground stems are well developed, usually bulbs, corms, tubers or rhizomes. This agrees with Genus Dianella as described by plantnet. Our Alfalfa family has inflorescences that clearly exceed the height of the leaf blades; leaf margins and midveins are scabrous at least at the base of the leaf; and grows in non-marine environments. Plants yellowish green or greyish green, with anthers longer than the expanded part of the filaments; fruit more than 4 mm long, shorter than or equal to its width; leaf margins smooth or minutely spiny. Leaf sheaths folded, usually with distinct keel-like ridges on the lower surface. Vein spacing on the lower surface of the leaf blade greater than or equal to the width of the veins, without papillae; anthers yellow, yellow-brown or blue. Leaf sheaths cover more than half. A comparison using plantnet's key locates Dianella caerulea, which is consistent with the results obtained by our previous plant identification software, so we deduce that this monocotyledon is Dianella caerulea. We found this plant in the right hand direction on Burns Rd at Picnic Point on our way into Georges River National Park. Given that Blue flax-lily occurs in a wide range of habitats and is easy to grow, I think it makes sense that it shows off in that area.

Very typical red *Oxalis*, including typical unlined perfect spiral basal trifoliate leaves, petioles with characteristic hairs, corolla fused from the bottom and 5 flower bases. Most importantly, after taking out a small amount of its leaves for tasting, it has a very typical sour taste of *Oxalis*, which suggests that it is a kind of *Oxalis*. Because its corolla is purple-red, based on experience, we judge that this is *Oxalis corymbosa*. Because the characteristics of the *Oxalidaceae* family are relatively complex, including not only *Oxalis corymbosa*, but also woody plants such as carambola, and the identification characteristics of this plant are too obvious, so we skipped the stage of using the key and directly identified this plant as *Oxalis corymbosa*. We found this *Oxalis corymbosa* by a road in the north of Panania. When we found it, it had only two flowers, and the distribution range was not large, and the settlement was isolated. Note: The clover of the Oxalis family and the clover of the Leguminosae family look different and have their own characteristics, so they can be distinguished. Although Oxalis latifolia is also similar to the plant we obtained, its compound leaves are shaped like arrows(or triangles), which is not align with the plant we found. Thus we can conclude that it is Oxalis corymbosa.

(Monocot) The number of flower bases is 6, indicating that the plant is a monocot. The flowers are whorled and arranged regularly, strictly related to the number of flower bases. The flowers are in the same perianth, showing strong characteristics of Liliales. After several identifications with plant identification software, it is almost certain that it is Colchicumaceae, a family that has recently branched from Liliaceae. Since there are no leaves, it is impossible to search through the key table of Colchicumaceae in plantnet, and Robinson Book does not even record this family (or maybe I can't find it), so we used the results of plant identification software to further search and found that Genus Burchardia is characterized by perennial herbs, smooth and hairless, with bulbs with papery scales, and tuberous roots. The leaves are mostly basal, 1 to 5, and folded. The scape is simple or has 1 to 4 branches, 1 to 4 bracts, and the inflorescence is umbrella-shaped, with up to 20 flowers or single flowers. The flowers are bisexual, with 6 tepals arranged in a whorl, similar and independent. There are 6 stamens, with anthers dorsifixed and split longitudinally, spreading outward. The ovary is superior, 3-chambered, with multiple ovules in each chamber, and the style is short and 3-lobed. The fruit is a capsule, with angular, brown seeds. In addition to these descriptions, the illustrations and pictures provided by plantnet also provide some hints. This information is almost completely consistent with our plant, with no discrepancies. So we think it belongs to the genus burchardia. Finally, since the only species of genus burchardia in NSW is Burchardia umbellata, we infer that this is Burchardia umbellata. This is also consistent with the results of the plant identification software.

This plant is in the Proteaceae family due to its alternatign pinnatisect leaves and inflorescences. In the genus Isopogon due to its spike-like inflorescence. I've identified it as Isopogon anemonifolius based on the leaf pattern and arrangement as well as the flowers matching the decription on Plantnet. Other plants have also been seen around the area. The other possible species is Isopogon anethifolius but I've excluded it because its leaves are too thin.

Very distinctive flowers and flower heads, the flower axis is shortened into a coiled inflorescence, and the leaves are alternate. There are four tepals, which is a very typical feature of Proteaceae. The plant has dense globose or cylindrical inflorescences, the flowers are sessile and closely arranged, and the bracts become woody when they bear fruit. The inflorescence axis is usually less than 5 cm, the fruits are radiate or bilaterally symmetrical nuts, and the leaves are usually divided into multiple segments or a few are entire. The fruit falls off with the bracts, the nut is not significantly flattened, the flower head is inflorescence, and the perianth tube is not completely split to the base. It is consistent with the description of the plantnet, and it can be judged that it belongs to the genus Isopogon. The leaves are usually divided into flat or cylindrical segments. In rare cases, the leaves below the inflorescence are intact, and the leaves are linear and less than 5 mm wide. The width of the divided segments of the leaves exceeds 1 mm and often exceeds 3 mm; the plant grows in an upright or spreading posture. The perianth is yellow and hairless except for a tuft of short hairs at the top. The leaves are usually no more than 9 cm long, the length of the undivided part is roughly equal to the divided part, the width of the divided part is 3-5 mm, usually only the midrib is obvious or all veins are not obvious, and the end is not sharp; the perianth length is about 10-12 mm, consistent with the description of the plantnet, it can be judged to be Isopogon anemonifolius. In addition, based on the comparison with the Proteaceae column in Robinson Book, we think our view is correct. The plant does have a very characteristic spherical woody cone, which is a typical feature of the genus isopogon. The height of its shrub is not high, just over one meter, so we can also rule out isopogon anetbifolius, which is taller (to 3m). So it can only be Isopogon anemonifolius.

This plant is of the myrtaceae family. This plant is woody with simply, entire leaves and a half-inferior ovary. There are oil glands on the leaves and has a distinctive smell. This plant is part of the Kunzea genera and is the species Kunzea ambigua. It matches the description in Robinson as it is a tall spreading shrub. The leaves are formed on short branchlets. It is a woody plant with aromatic leaves and the fruit forms a single capsule. These flowers are white with multiple, somewhat showy stamens.
In a reveg area near Wolli Creek.

[All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the Myrtaceae family; woody shrub, simple entire leaves with oil glands, actinomorphic flowers with 5 petals, a half inferior ovary and numerous showy stamens. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the Genus Kunzea; dehiscent fruit, flower buds without calyptras, free stamens that exceed petals in length, alternate leaves, thin leaves (<5mm wide), persistent sepals and flowers on leaf axils. Although Genus Kunzea and Leptospermum appear similar, the filaments of Kunzea exceed petal length unlike Leptospermum (filaments shorter than petals), hence why the plant is Genus Kunzea. Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Kunzea ambigua; white flowers crowded near leaves, short pedicels and villous young stems. While Kunzea axillaris and Kunzea occidentalis are similar to K. ambigua, K. axillaris has far shorter leaves (3-5mm compared to 4-12mm) and K. occidentalis has more glabrous young stems. Extra Info: K. ambigua has a distinctly strong and enjoyable smell. Also, Les Robinson speculates that the term "ambigua" (meaning doubt in Latin) indicates the founders' original confusion with this species regarding its classification as Kunzea or Leptospermum. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

It can be directly judged from the appearance of the flower that it belongs to the Fabaceae Fabaceae subfamily. The leaves of the plant are all single leaves, simple, degenerate or missing. The two teeth on the upper part of the sepals are not fused into a wide notched lip, and the three teeth on the lower part are very small and narrow. The bracteoles are large, rounded, and easy to fall off; the leaves are tiny and also easy to fall off. The leaves are linear, sometimes oblong or narrowly ovate, and are 1 to 5 mm wide. The upper surface of the leaves has a distinct reticular texture. After comparing it with plantnet, I can confirm that it is Mirbelia rubiifolia. In addition, using Robinson Book to search under the genus Mirbelia in the leguminous family, I can find that there are only two plants, and the other plant is a slender, erect shrub, and 1m high, which is completely different from the plant I obtained, so it can be ruled out. [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the Fabaceae family; woody shrub, legumes as fruit and flowers with 5 free petals. This plant is of the Fabaceae subfamily, Caesalpinioideae as the flowers are irregular with a non-papilionaceous corolla and equally sized petals. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the Genus Senna; absent spines/prickles, pinnately compound leaves, yellow petals and flat dehiscent pods. Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Senna didymobotrya; 7-15 leaflet pairs per leaf, absent glands on leaves, tall raceme inflorescence with dark brown bracts, 2 conspicuous anthers and oblong pods with depressions between the seeds. All other Senna species do not have as tall of a raceme and have much lighter coloured bracts. Extra info: This plant is commonly referred to as the popcorn plant as rubbing the leaves will bring about the scent of buttered popcorn, however, it does depend on the person. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

[All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the family Solanaceae; woody shrub, purple flowers with 5 petals and berries as fruit. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the genus Solanum; pinnatisect leaves, firm berries and stellate, purple, 5 lobed flowers in a cymose/panicle-like inflorescence (Fig 5). Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Solanum aviculare; non-climbing, erect, light violet corolla, entire margins with leaf length at 2-8 times as its width, leaves are either lobed or entire with a stalk, egg-shaped berries and mostly glabrous on all surfaces. This species is commonly confused with Solanum laciniatum. However, the above pictures show no notches in the corolla lobes. It is also confused with Solanum vescum which unlike S. aviculare has a spherical shaped berry and stalkless leaves. Unfortunately, the berries aren’t ripe, and the final colour isn’t known to be able to effectively use the key. Hence the focus is on the berries shape and leaves. Extra info: The common name, Kangaroo apple is inspired by the shape of the leaves which is thought to resemble a kangaroo’s foot. Whilst the scientific name ‘aviculare’ refers to little bird in Latin after the wing-like appendages on the leaves. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

Using the description provided by PlantNET the plant would be: In the family Solanaceae due to it having simple pinnate leaves that are alternate, a calyx that is campanulate and a five lobed corolla that is stellate. In the genus Solanum because there appears to be 5 stamens that each have anthers that are 2-locular and basifixed. In image 4 the 5 stamens may be difficult to confirm, however the angle of the image and the symmetry of the plant could allow me to infer that the remaining 2 stamens were out of shot. For the presence of there being 2 locular and basifixed anthers, the apparent bulge and openings of the anthers in image 5 is shown through the white outline that shows that there are two parts. This also shows that the bulge that divides the two appears to align between the stamen beneath them, which can help confirm that there are 5 stamens in total through the number of 2-locular anthers. In the species Solanum aviculare because it’s an erect shrub, has a violet corolla, entire leaves, and lacks prickles. I’ve rejected Solanum linearifolium as an option as it is not glabrous. I’ve also rejected Solanum vescum because the size of the leaf is different with our plant not having a measurement of 5 to 15 cm long and 0.5 to 1.3 cm wide.

[All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the family Commelinaceae; herbaceous monocot with conspicuous flowers in parts of 3 (6 tepals in 2 whorls of 3), a superior ovary and parallel veins in leaves. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the genus Tradescantia; multiple pedicellate flower clusters enclosed with 2 large leafy bracts. Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Tradescantia fluminensis; the dark green top surface of the leaves, the lighter green underside of the leaves, 3 free white inner tepals, 3 green outer tepals, 6 yellow anthers on filaments tufted with white hairs and no occurrence of fruit. It is unlikely to be the species Tradescantia zebrina which has pink tepals and purple on the underside of its leaves. Extra info: While amazing for groundcover, this plant is not ideal for native species conservation. The competitiveness of this plant has been incredibly damaging to our native habitats and plants. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.
